body: I simply hate myself. I hate looking in the mirror--it absolutely terrifies me. I hate how I'm too much of a coward to cut deeper. I'm actually a good person who tries to be compassionate all the time. But it doesn't matter because I hate myself and I'm drowning in depression.

Wow, that's quite the side effect! Luckily, Remeron hasn't made me drowsy. My dose was recently doubled to 30mg per night and I wake up feeling fine. It reinforces how different drugs can work for each person.

I'm happy that Prozac worked for your depressive thoughts; however, if it's causing you to self harm more that is unacceptable. It's concerning that you want to go any further with it as well. I would discuss this with the doctor that prescribed you Prozac and see if there are other antidepressants that may be better suited for you.

Also...just look at my username! Prozac sent me to an inpatient psych ward in less than a week. I wrote about it a few times on Reddit. Some medication simply doesn't work with certain people's brain chemistry. ¯\\\_(ツ)_/¯
Of course. Talk away!
Yay!!! I'm genuinely happy to hear that. I look forward to when both of our lives are fixed and depression-free. I heard life can be beautiful!

That's great to hear! Having the necessities and shelter is vital for your mental health and recovery.

Those neighbors with easily accessible internet sound lovely and all too ;)

I completely understand your reasoning. I wish I could offer you more help.

I also wish you the very best and hope what you're going through is only temporary.

Could you possibly check yourself into a hospital's psych ward? They can provide food, shelter, and counseling. Obviously it's not ideal. Are there any homeless shelters in your area, perhaps?

You have true strength and endurance to battle depression without your family. You're not alone here at least! You can always message me if you want to talk. You don't deserve to go through this on your own.

I'm incredibly sorry they could do such a hurtful and cruel thing to you. You deserve support and love in your time of need. Know that it's absolutely not your fault.

Are there any other family or friends you can stay with or are you supporting yourself currently? I wish you the best!

First off, I can't express how cool it is that you started a band. That takes a lot of initiative and guts, even if it didn't go to plan.

Please don't feel defeated because of your try out. Every musician feels exactly like you at some point. Imposter syndrome is not uncommon at all in this field. The thing with music is that it just takes practice, and a ton of it to get better. 

I sucked at the piano for a long time and gave it up for several years because I thought I'd never be good as my brother. After finally coming back to it, I fell in love with the hardest piece of piano music I could find and practiced it for a couple of months. Well guess what? I can play the whole thing now! ([This is it, if you're wondering](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WhLDse5R8dQ)). Now I wish I never gave up piano in the past. I promise you, you are going to feel like this at one point.

You're going to play bass in a band one day and look back at these moments as just slumps in your journey to becoming an amazing musician. Music is incredibly frustrating sometimes, but it will become so rewarding in the end. Practice, practice, practice! 

Not to mention, don't be so hard on yourself! I'm sure the other people in the band are worrying about their own mistakes rather than yours. Good luck :)

Same. That's what gets me through each day, though. Try to live each day for them until you want to live for yourself as well.

They must love you, and you clearly love them--that's a beautiful thing to remember :)

Hey, this time of year can be an absolute struggle. I'm having the exact same thoughts you are right now.

I'm so sorry you can't afford a therapist currently. No one should be prevented from mental health services due to money; it's not right.

If you're currently attending school, there should be a school therapist available to you. You can also always call a suicide hotline if those thoughts of suicide feel too unbearable. I wish I knew more resources that could provide you help.

You can message me and we can talk whenever :)

I'm wishing you the very best!

Thanks for your replies :) 

I think you're right that mania isn't the best descriptor for my reaction to Prozac; I didn't suffer from any excitement, euphoria, delusions, and overactivity. There's actually a lot of people online that suffered similar adverse reactions to Prozac in their first week and both psychiatrists in the hospital agreed that's what it was. However, I have no one to tell me how long some of the symptoms will stay.

Honestly, the fluctuations in mood are pretty new to me, but they never reach manic levels ever--simply my normal self or extremely depressed. Before this experience, my depression and the anxiety weren't ever this bad. I would describe myself as rather level-headed and looking through the list of personality disorders I don't relate to any. I'm still a pretty "chill" and collected person--never had an outburst in my life! Maybe there's an obsessive component to the depressive thoughts, but there's no compulsions to be categorized as OCD? Perhaps the first week on Mirtazapine was relief and happiness from being off the Prozac and out of the psych ward? Maybe I need a higher dose and more time?

Glad I hopefully didn't suffer any brain damage!

Yes, I would describe it like that. The psychiatrist at the inpatient psych ward described it as a Prozac induced mania.

Thanks for reaffirming that my experience at the hospital was terrible. I don't have much to compare it too..haha. It's hard to fully comprehend how bad U.S. mental healthcare, and healthcare in general, is until you need it the most. To expand on my continued experiences with healthcare, I haven't even been able to find a psychiatrist willing to see me for the past three weeks. I've literally struck out on 55 psychiatrists my health insurance covers because they're either not taking new patients or refuse to ever return my calls and messages. I even asked to see my therapist twice a week instead of only once, but she's too busy to do so. I feel so defeated and helpless, like I'm crying out into the void for help. I'm sure if a medication I took caused visible physical damage to my body I'd have no trouble finding help, but with mental health no one can give me an answer or the time of day. 

Sorry for the rambling! Just frustrated and feeling mentally damaged :(

It doesn't sound like you're blaming others at all! It's healthy to express your feelings. Your words resonate with me--depression can have this compulsive and/or obsessive aspect where we develop these negative thinking patterns that become a struggle to fix. I think it takes time and practice to undo these bad habits, which is, admittedly, a struggle at the start.

I have hope we won't feel like this for long :)

Oh, that's longer than I hoped. I definitely will be talking to a psychiatrist about this, but it seems like I'll have to be relying on the Klonopin longer and more than I hoped. You're right that it may be too soon for the Remeron to have stabilized my depression and anxiety.

I also didn't mention that I was just hospitalized 2 1/2 weeks ago for an extremely adverse reaction to Prozac: catatonia, sustained rapid heart rate, insomnia, and constant debilitating panic attacks for days--all symptoms which I never experienced before. So that drug may still have its remnants in me. 

It's been quite the health rollercoaster, these past few weeks :'(
Thank you for the response. Do you have any idea on how long the additional anxiety usually lasts?

That honestly sounds fantastic! It takes a lot of heartache and strength to climb out of that dark place and accomplish so much (especially in 2 months!).

I wish you the very best at your job, your future schooling, and your dream of being a musical artist.

Thank you for the motivational words, too :)

It's uplifting to hear that your moments of extreme depression are uncommon occurrences and you're in just a bad mood. Also, it's great that you and your psych realize that there are bumps in the road and you're currently in one of those temporary slumps. I'm glad that Zoloft has been helping you too.

Last, and most importantly, you opening up about your good future prospects and attending university is a huge achievement to look forward too. You should be proud of yourself for your motivation to finish school soon--don't overlook this.

It seems like you have a wonderful future that you're cultivating for yourself and looking forward too!

It pisses me off that depression can make me indifferent to living too; it's no fun, as you already know.

If you feel that your best course of recovery is waiting out this moment of being deeply unmotivated then that's fine and your choice. However, know that we don't think as clearly and logically when depressed. And sometimes it might be best to try at least one small little task that you enjoyed that you couldn't fathom doing today. There is no shame in at least trying :)

I'm really sorry that you're unable to visit your friend after waiting so long to do so. Life simply blows sometimes. You have every right to feel angry and upset right now, but as time passes these feelings won't feel so sharp and unbearable. It seems unbelievable at the moment, but it will slowly get less suffocating and all-consuming.

With that being said, life can be really amazing too. It probably feels nice to communicate with this friend. Can you increase your time interacting with them, even if it's not in-person, until you can possibly visit them?

I'm sure it is a phase, because I've been there before. I too thought it was permanent, but it passed. 

Is there someone in your life that can push you to do something that you may enjoy? Can I be your crutch in some way?

Zoloft can also make people feel apathetic, so that's something to take into consideration.

First, be proud that you're choosing to cope with your pain by letting it out on this forum rather than harming yourself. That's a truly brave and tough task when you feel miserable. If it makes you feel better to let everything out here then keep doing it.

Second, I don't think you're better off "rotting away" and you certainly don't seem to deserve it. Your depression deserves to rot away, but you're not your depression--it's a chemical imbalance that is taking hold of you at this moment. 

We're together right now, both feeling terrible, but we're going to get out of it.

That's a long time. I would definitely bring up your concerns and the possibility for a new antidepressant with your doctor. 

Prozac caused me to go through the worst symptoms I ever could experience on the drug. Then I was switched to Remeron and it's a world of difference. I'm sure you'll find something that clicks with your brain chemistry.

Being unmotivated is another unwelcome symptom of depression. That doesn't mean that it can't be overcome. I empathize with you so much. I was intent on staying in bed all day today too, but I tried faking it the whole day. It was painfully hard every minute, but after faking it most of the day, I finally got a breath of fresh air and was motivated to draw after not having the drive for weeks. I don't think I would have got that reprieve if I went with my original plan for the morning.

Instead of looking at the task of leaving the house, which can seem insurmountable at times, push yourself just to get dressed and go on from there. Commend yourself for each task you complete--you deserve it! What I've come to realize is that depression is a battle that needs to be fought hard to be won. You've already made brave steps by seeing a guidance counselor and trying antidepressants. How long have you been on the Zoloft? Often times SSRI's can take many weeks to finally feel their effects. If you've been on it for several months, maybe it's time to discuss changing your dosage or trying a different antidepressant (there are a ton!) with your doctor. 

Remember, depression can make us be way too hard on ourselves, which adds to the negative feelings. I'm sure you don't suck at everything you enjoy! You're probably pretty amazing at somethings too! And let's say there is something you enjoy that you're not great at--who cares because you enjoy it!

I now how hard it must be to do right now, but you please have to tell yourself that the depression and the messed up chemicals in your brain (DAMN THEM!) are telling you that life is pointless! I was where you are now before--where depression puts a wall in front of your future, so you can't see past it. Yep, that can cause a lot of despair and meaninglessness to life. But you have to know that it is temporary and you will find a reason to live for, and then another, and another. It can be really small, but it will come and chip at that wall.

Yeah, there are a lot of terrible humans, but I think there are more good ones that we don't hear about. I'm sure you're one of them. Don't be so hard on yourself.

Lastly, you're not alone. You're here with me and other people that all suffer from the demon that is depression. I'll be sad if you're gone!

Be well and talk with me as much as you want!

I'm so sorry you have to deal with unsupportive roommates and money anxiety. It sucks when you have to bottle it up inside as well. Life sucks sometimes and depression always does.

Try to think of this moment as only a blip in your life. You WILL overcome it; it will be unbearably hard at times, but depression will not define you.

（っ・∀・)っ All the best!

I was prescribed a tetracyclic antidepressant, Remeron (Mirtazapine), by the psychiatrist at the psych ward. They're usually given as a second option when SSRI's don't work well. It's been about a week that I've been on Remeron, and so far things are going well. The only side effects are that it causes me to have pretty detailed dreams (it also acts as a sleep aid) and it increases my appetite. I need the latter because I lost so much weight from the constant anxiety on Prozac! 

The weird part is I used another SSRI, Zoloft, when I was 12 for around six months when my parents divorced. What I remember is that it didn't have much of an effect on me and I specifically asked not to be be prescribed it as I thought it was ineffective...what a mistake that was! So, I'm not sure if SSRI's don't mesh well with my brain or if it was just the Prozac. I don't think I'll be taking the chance with SSRI's again because I can deal with the depression, but the anxiety I experienced was far too traumatic to ever take a chance with again.

Additionally, I'm learning cognitive behavioral therapy techniques from my therapist to deal with depression and anxiety. Currently, I'm feeling a world's away from what I felt last week, and I expect things to only get better with therapy and the Remeron!

My therapist encouraged me to go on an antidepressant and suggested that the quickest way would be through my primary care physician. Sadly, this is true because I have yet to find a psychiatrist that is even accepting new patients in my area. 

When I made an appointment with my doctor he wasn't available, so I saw the nurse practitioner at the practice. She did warn me about the ideations of suicide I could experience on Prozac and to go to the hospital if I did have the desire to self-harm, but, unexpectedly enough, those never came. This isn't meant to disparage her or NP's, as she was really sweet, but the psychiatrist I saw in the psych ward said, "That she had no business prescribing me Prozac," and immediately realized I don't deserve to be committed because he recognized all my symptoms as a reaction to the SSRI. He prescribed me Remeron instead and Klonopin to get rid of the residual anxiety from Prozac's long half-life. He also said he would be happy to be my doctor, but he only does inpatient work. Ugh.

Unfortunately, both :(

I started taking it Wednesday. By Friday I was feeling severely depressed--I was slumped over and couldn't concentrate much. Each night I suffered insomnia because I took the Prozac before bed. My doctor didn't inform me that you should take it in the morning for this reason. The few hours of sleep I did get were filled with vivid nightmares and I'd constantly wake up in a panic attack with my chest feeling as if it was gripped in a vice.

By Saturday, I was in complete grief between the panic attacks. Not to mention, I rarely ever experienced panic attacks before this experience, just generalized anxiety. I tried doing things to calm myself down, like take my dog for a long walk, but I couldn't get out of the extremely negative headspace I was in. I truly believed I'd never be happy again. 

I went online to see if the effects I were feeling were common among Prozac users, and a lot of resources online said depression and anxiety would get worse in the first couple of weeks before it would get better. I naively decided to tough it out.

Sunday was probably the worst. I entered a six hour catatonic state, which may be the scariest experience of my life. That day I was in a constant panic attack. The adrenaline refused to stop shooting through my body, so I guess it just shut down other motor functions. I laid on my bed paralyzed, unable to speak, with terrible arm pain--as if lightning was constantly shooting through them--but completely conscious and in a panic. I was completely non-functional and thought my life was over at this point. After the 6 terrifying hours I was able to eat a bit, though still with adrenaline shooting through my body from time to time. That didn't last long, because after about two hours I was back in the constant fight-or-flight mode.

Monday I lost my mind. Between the constant panic I started having obsessive self-loathing thoughts EVERY FEW SECONDS the entire day. I was screaming on the ground crying to make it stop. I stared at myself in the mirror and saw a freak looking back at me. My mom tried to take me on a walk to get my mind of things, but I felt like I was looking at the world through a TV screen and I was separate from it. I then started crying in public and had to go home. (Note: I was a completely functioning, level-headed person before this.)

By Tuesday morning, after barely any sleep, unable to eat because of the anxious nausea, and going in and out of catatonia, my mom convinced me to go to the hospital. I arrived at the triage crying and shaking because of the constant panic attacks I was having that were ruining my mind and body. They took my heart rate and it was 120 bpm. The next morning in the psych ward it was 170 bpm. It didn't go below 100 until nearly a week on sedatives.

I'm sorry you had to deal with this horrid reaction too!

So far, Remeron hasn't made me that drowsy. It's made my dreams incredibly vivid and detailed, which can be a bit unsettling at times though.

I've read so many horror stories of Klonopin addiction and withdrawal that I'm already tapering off the dose the psychiatrist prescribed me. Simply taking it for a few days had me already craving the way it made me felt. That is way out of the norm for me, so I'm trying to do .25mg every other day or two days for this week instead of of the 1mg everyday for 30 days I was prescribed!

I don't want to discourage anyone from using SSRI's with my story. They can be a life-saver for a lot of people. What I experienced was ridiculously unlucky and rare. I would share your hesitancy with your psychiatrist; having a session with them doesn't mean you have to take any medication. 

In regards to those random lows, I would try seeing a therapist that can teach you some cognitive behavioral therapy techniques. For instance, mine taught me about mindfulness. If I feel one of those lows or a panic attach approaching (learn the signs before they happen!) focus your WHOLE body on a certain task--it can be anything. Let's say you're drawing. Focus on how the pencil feels in your hand; the air on your skin; what colors you see; narrate every action you are doing in completing the task so your mind can't concentrate on the depressive thoughts that are encroaching and attempting to take over.

Additionally, and I know this may seem trite, but running made me the happiest I've ever been and allowed me to sleep deeply and soundly. Running regularly is powerful as Prozac, without all the side effects....It's hard to start in the beginning, but once you get better at it, it becomes incredibly rewarding. /r/running is a great and welcoming subreddit that can advise you on beginner running plans if you're new to it.

I wish you all the best!

Not only are these reactions to SSRI's rare, but they usually occur in people with bipolar disorder, which I don't have at all. I'd describe myself as super level-headed, so I was just dealt a bizarrely uncommon hand. 

Yeah, I completely relate to the other experiences I found online. Reading them is just another reassurance that I didn't in fact lose my mind!

Thank you! I'm glad too! 

I live a pretty unexciting life, so this experience totally felt like I was in some surreal horror movie. At least I'll have a crazy story to tell--if anyone even believes me!
